A compiler narrates Ruiyan Shiyan’s daily calling to the one in charge and self-response; another record quotes the call directly. Dongshan Liangjie asks which one is his interlocutor’s person in charge and rejects the readily responding person as an answer. Tianru Weize explicitly says that mind, on each person’s own share, is called oneself and also the one in charge. Zhongfeng Mingben groups Ruiyan’s designation with Linji Yixuan’s true person of no rank, while Yulin Tongxiu warns against taking bright identity-consciousness as realization of it. Zhaozhou Congshen says it is no other person and warns against seeking outside. The label therefore functions as something called, located, equated, and tested, not as an unexamined modern theory of self.

Senses.Explanation: A living phrase is a phrase the records describe as not caught in verbal explanation, a fixed reasoning track, thought, or deliberation. One direct definition is contrastive: “Speech containing speech is called a dead phrase; speech without speech is called a living phrase.” Another says that a phrase which does not fall into verbal explanation, does not drop into a track of reasoning, does not enter thought, does not permit deliberation, changes a thousand and ten thousand ways, and meets opposition on eight sides is called a living phrase. Gulin Qingmao records another description: “As for its living: a net will not hold it, a call will not turn its head, the ancient sages do not arrange it, and to this day it has no place.” A recurrent instruction says, “Investigate the living phrase; do not investigate the dead phrase.” Blue Cliff Record says that recognition under a living phrase is never forgotten, whereas recognition under a dead phrase cannot save oneself. Records also ask “What is a living phrase?” and preserve different answers, including “obtained within death.” An intermediate category, “a phrase neither dead nor living,” also occurs. These are the records' descriptions and classifications; the entry does not infer a hidden force behind them.

Ruibai Mingxue pairs the expression with ‘round and complete’ and says it appears throughout the myriad forms; Yuan’an Liao joins it to ‘turning and rolling’ where there is no place to approach or grasp. The adjective also operates on concrete teaching objects: Baichi Xingyuan calls his staff lively as a dragon, and Konggu Daocheng says the staff comes alive in his hand and rouses the assembly. The explicitly unnamed questioner in Feiyin Tongrong’s record applies it to what is already complete in each person. Different objects receive the same appraisal; the evidence does not establish several different things or a hidden symbolic sense.

Senses.Explanation: Nostrils reaching the sky is an extravagant bodily picture used as a conspicuous appraisal. Chan records put it into an answer, a self-image, an unnamed monk’s alternative question, and a challenge whose appearance would put Tianyi Yihuai’s own life at stake; those varied jobs do not establish one hidden psychological state. Chongsheng Xie answers the condition after the antelope has hung up its horns with “nostrils reaching the sky.” Yunmen Wenyan ends a hall address by saying that on meeting a person his nostrils reach the sky. Puan Yinsu names himself in the image amid a sequence in which each figure occupies an impossible place. Tianyi Yihuai says that if anyone now appeared with sky-reaching nostrils, his own life would be in danger. Feiyin Tongrong and Shiqi Tongyun reuse the phrase in later independent records, showing that the appraisal travels beyond Tianyi Yihuai’s record.
